papers.title: ESCAPE: Egocentric Sensing for Collision Avoidance and Policy Execution
papers.abstract: Motion planning in unstructured environments is a bottleneck for robot deployment. Current visuomotor policies predominantly rely on external cameras, introducing perceptual blind spots and fragility due to occlusions, clutter, and calibration constraints. To overcome these limitations, we propose ESCAPE, an online egocentric sensing framework for collision-free trajectory generation. ESCAPE aggregates sparse measurements from distributed depth sensors, converting them into a structured, obstacle-aware point cloud representation. Our policy leverages a flow matching-based generative framework, and trains on a high-quality dataset comprising over 100K safety-critical trajectories. With joint optimization of goal-reaching and collision objectives, it produces safe trajectories directly from these egocentric inputs. Crucially, ESCAPE is trained entirely in simulation and transfers zero-shot to physical hardware without any real-world fine-tuning. Extensive simulation and real-world evaluations demonstrate that ESCAPE achieves stable motion planning using only egocentric perception, outperforming external-view and voxelized-planning baselines across both simulation and real-world evaluations.

papers.title: PrismPlan: A Shared GPU Substrate for Motion Planning Across Paradigms
papers.abstract: GPU acceleration has made motion planning one to two orders of magnitude faster, but it has not made the three paradigms---sampling, search, and optimization---comparable to one another: every GPU-accelerated planner is built around a single paradigm, so comparing across libraries also compares their collision checkers. All three, however, bottleneck on the same GPU primitive: batched collision detection and the batched forward kinematics beneath it. PrismPlan builds that primitive once, as a shared substrate of per-sphere collision--kinematics device code that every planner consumes. Because they all execute the same device code, the backend is held fixed by construction and the paradigms can be compared head-to-head. We run six planners over 1800 MotionBenchMaker problems on three robots (7--14 DoF, one a dual-arm whole-body composite) at an equal 2s budget. On the 7-DoF Panda, sampling (pRRTC) is the most reliable paradigm at 98%, while parallel search (wPA*SE) follows within four points at a 3-4 times$ lower median latency, and the local optimizers trail well behind when made to solve from scratch. On the 14-DoF dual-arm composite, sampling still solves about 90% of feasible problems, while no search or optimization planner clears a third of them. Our open-source code is available at https://github.com/XiaoyubotMotionTeam/PrismPlan.

papers.title: A Heterogeneous UAV UGV Methodology for Aerial Tracking of Mini Autonomous Cars
papers.abstract: Aerial tracking of autonomous ground vehicles can provide useful situational awareness in environments where fixed external perception infrastructure is unavailable. However, visual-only tracking from an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) is limited by camera field of view, viewpoint changes, occlusions, and temporary loss of target visibility. This paper presents a heterogeneous UAV--UGV methodology for aerial tracking of small-scale autonomous ground vehicles in simulation. The system is implemented in ROS~2 and Gazebo Sim using a Tello-like UAV equipped with a front-facing RGB camera and multiple LIMO-like unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs). Three approaches are evaluated: a training-free color-marker baseline, a YOLO-based visual baseline, and a proposed UAV--UGV fusion method. The proposed method uses the same visual detector as the YOLO baseline, but combines visual detections with UGV state information to maintain the target estimate during visual gaps. The methods are evaluated across four scenarios: single-car tracking, crossing trajectories, occlusion, and UAV-assisted awareness. Results over 600 simulation runs show that the proposed fusion method achieves nearly continuous track coverage across all scenarios while reducing localization error relative to the YOLO baseline. Compared with the visual-only YOLO approach, the fusion method reduces RMSE by 37.3\%, 64.2\%, 62.6\%, and 61.8\% in the four evaluated scenarios, respectively. The method also enables conflict-awareness lead times of 10.20~s in the crossing scenario and 9.07~s in the UAV-assisted awareness scenario. These results indicate that heterogeneous UAV--UGV fusion can improve aerial tracking continuity and robustness when visual observations are intermittent.

papers.title: Context-Aware RGB-Thermal-Radar Obstacle Perception for Resource-Constrained ASVs
papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle perception is challenging for small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs): reflections and glare confound visible-light cameras, vessel motion shifts the apparent waterline, and darkness removes the dominant sensing modality altogether. Rather than treating multimodal fusion as a static accuracy gain, we propose a context-aware architecture that combines RGB and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) mmWave radar, and inertial context. A bearing-sector interface provides the navigation controller with calibrated obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status. It also distinguishes sensor dropout from a valid observation with no detected obstacle. Using new multimodal lake recordings, we deployed the pipeline in a 24-leg closed-loop pilot under uncontrolled lake conditions (16 day, 4 dusk, and 4 night; 351 m), including night legs in which RGB was unusable and the vessel drove on LWIR and radar evidence alone. On eight held-out low-light recordings, the calibrated fusion model achieved average precision (AP) 0.869 and expected calibration error 0.108, compared with AP 0.673 for rule-based fusion, 0.620 for gated fusion, and 0.903 for RGB alone. Our results expose a central tradeoff: RGB ranks best when usable, whereas fusion preserves a navigation input when RGB fails. This work is a step toward perception that remains usable and degrades predictably across multi-day ASV missions.

papers.title: EvoAD: Self-Evolving Autonomous Driving via Latent World-Model Guided Post-hoc Reflection
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving systems have achieved rapid progress by learning unified policies that map sensor observations directly to driving trajectories. However, once deployed, these systems typically remain frozen: they may repeat similar decisions in similar scenes, and failures can only be addressed through costly data collection and retraining. This sharply contrasts with human drivers, who improve lifelong through experience, memory, and reflection. In this work, we ask whether autonomous driving systems can achieve similar post-deployment self-evolution to human drivers. We propose EvoAD, a self-evolving autonomous driving framework via latent world-model guided post-hoc reflection. EvoAD stores driving experiences in a bird's-eye-view feature memory pool, retrieves scene-relevant precedents according to geometric and semantic similarity, and uses a latent world model to evaluate the future consequences of candidate trajectories in a compact planning-oriented space. Instead of treating memory as external textual contexts or using world models only for pre-action simulation, EvoAD transforms executed driving outcomes into reusable improvement signals for future decisions. This enables the system to diagnose how prior trajectories could have been improved and to refine behavior in similar future scenarios without retraining the base driving policy. Experiments on NAVSIM v1 and v2 show consistent improvements across reflection rounds and state-of-the-art performance, demonstrating the potential of world models as reflective mechanisms for post-deployment self-evolution in autonomous driving.

papers.title: COMPARATIVE CRITICAL ANALYSIS OF URBAN DESIGN PROCESSES IN TWO PLANNING SYSTEMS IN SAUDI ARABIA: CASE STUDIES OF THE WATERFRONT DEVELOPMENT IN JEDDAH AND YANBU
papers.abstract: This research critically examines the urban design processes within two distinct planning systems in Saudi Arabia, focusing on the waterfront developments in Jeddah and Yanbu. It explores how decision-making environments, governance mechanisms, and the roles of various actors influence the quality of urban public spaces. Despite substantial urbanisation driven by development programs, research on design governance and the influence of the design process on urban space quality in Saudi Arabia remains limited. This gap necessitates a deeper understanding of how governance frameworks shape urban design outcomes and their alignment with national developmental objectives. Employing a comparative framework and a case study approach, the study evaluates the centralised, dependent planning system of Jeddah and the independent system of Yanbu, highlighting their strengths and weaknesses in delivering high-quality urban design aligned with Saudi Vision 2030 and related development programs. Using theories of design governance and planning culture, this dissertation develops a conceptual framework focused on design principles, tools, mechanisms, and actor interactions in urban development. Primary data were collected through in-depth interviews, document analysis, and field observations, revealing systemic disparities in governance approaches. Findings reveal that while Jeddah’s flexibility-driven planning model often leads to inconsistency, Yanbu’s prescriptive model provides stability but lacks adaptability. This analysis underscores the need for an integrated approach that combines the strengths of both systems to enhance the effectiveness of urban design governance. The study contributes valuable insights into the local and global discourse on urban planning by providing lessons on aligning governance frameworks with sustainable urban development goals, particularly in rapidly urbanizing contexts.

papers.title: Mapping crown length and canopy depth across global forests at 1 km from multi-platform lidar and satellite data
papers.abstract: Crown length (CL) describes the vertical extent of an individual tree's live crown. Canopy depth (CD) describes the vertical extent of the canopy within a forest stand. Both inform fire behaviour, vegetation and habitat models, yet their global distributions remain poorly resolved. We present global maps of mean CL and CD at 1 km resolution for 2020. We first retrieved CL for individual trees segmented from lidar point clouds, as tree height minus crown-base height. Within each of 1147 reference records on six continents, mean CL was the average of the tree values and CD was the 95th-percentile tree height minus the lowest crown base. Both were related to satellite and environmental predictors using random forest models. Tree-level CL agreed with field measurements and manual annotations with R² = 0.62 and RMSE = 2.63 m. Across 46 validation plots, RMSE was 1.90 m for mean CL and 2.09 m for CD. In the 30 % hold-out set, the mapping models achieved R² = 0.64 for CL and 0.72 for CD, with RMSE of 2.15 m and 2.98 m. Global mean CL and CD were 7.0 m and 14.2 m. Long crowns and deep canopies occurred in equatorial rain forests and humid temperate forests. Savannas, Mediterranean woodlands and dry forests had the smallest values. These maps give the first globally consistent view of the crown layer beneath the canopy top. They can constrain crown geometry in vegetation models, canopy fuel depth in fire models and vertical habitat structure in biodiversity studies.

papers.title: Living with the Foreign Agents’ Law: a socio-legal analysis of Russian human rights defenders’ responses to the Foreign Agents’ Law, 2012-2024
papers.abstract: This thesis argues that Russian human rights defenders’ responses to the Foreign Agents’ Law reveal a polyvocal and context-dependent legal consciousness that challenges the universal applicability of dominant legal consciousness frameworks. By putting legal culture and legal consciousness approaches into dialogue, it re-theorises legal consciousness outside the North American context, showing how Russian activists simultaneously reproduce and resist dominant legal meanings to generate a more situated understanding of law’s role under increasing authoritarianism. Introduced in 2012, the Foreign Agents’ Law regulates non-profit organisations based on funding sources and activities. Over the next decade, it became a central tool of civil society repression, particularly targeting human rights organisations. Those designated ‘foreign agents’ faced onerous reporting requirements and reputational harm, the term itself evoking Cold War-era espionage. Amendments since 2019 expanded the law’s scope, making legal compliance ever more difficult. By 2022, many human rights defenders chose to kinut’ Rossiiu (“quit Russia”), many continuing their work in exile. The Supreme Court ordered the liquidation of International Memorial and Memorial Human Rights Centre, signalling the law’s function as a mechanism of systemic suppression. This thesis employs a socio-legal approach, combining doctrinal analysis, social media and documentary review, and interviews with human rights defenders. Using Ewick and Silbey’s (1998) heuristics of ‘before,’ ‘with,’ and ‘against’ the law, together with Fritsvold’s (2009) ‘under the law,’ I developed a four-part framework for analysing human rights defenders’ responses. I also interrogate the transferability of the legal consciousness framework to the Russian context, integrating insights from legal culture scholarship and ‘cultural dissent’ to emphasise the contested, dynamic nature of legal meaning-making. Empirical observations show that human rights defenders oscillated between multiple legal positions, sometimes within a single utterance, for example, mobilising legal complaints ‘before the law’ while simultaneously expressing scepticism toward legal institutions. These observations underpin the thesis’s argument that understanding legal consciousness requires attention to its shifting, context-dependent character and the polyvocality of legal narratives employed by a range of human rights actors

papers.title: A global 1 km forest crown base height dataset for 2020 from multi-platform lidar and satellite data
papers.abstract: Crown base height (CBH) is the height of the lowest living branch of a tree. It marks where the live crown begins, and it is a key input for forest growth, vegetation and fire behaviour models. However, a global-scale map of CBH is still lacking. We mapped the first global maps of two stand-level CBH metrics at 1 km resolution for 2020. CBH was first estimated for individual trees segmented from airborne, drone, terrestrial and backpack lidar point clouds. The tree values were then aggregated to 1432 plots of 1 km × 1 km on six continents, and two plot-level metrics were derived. CBHwa is the mean weighted by the square of tree height, which follows the canopy-forming trees. CBHmin is the minimum, which marks the lower edge of the live canopy. Random forest models related both metrics to 47 satellite and environmental predictors. Tree-level CBH agreed with field measurements and manual annotations of 1641 trees with an RMSE of 3.32 m. Plot-level RMSE was 2.65 m for CBHwa and 1.80 m for CBHmin. The models reached R2 = 0.80 (RMSE 2.40 m) for CBHwa and R2 = 0.65 (RMSE 1.51 m) for CBHmin. Global mean CBHwa and CBHmin are 9.5 m and 3.8 m. CBHwa is highest in tropical moist forests, whereas CBHmin is highest in boreal forests. These maps provide a consistent global reference of CBH for forest management, vegetation modelling and wildfire risk assessment.
